Sample Size Planning for Accuracy in Parameter Estimation for Reliability Coefficients

Source: R/ss_aipe_reliability.R
ss_aipe_reliability.Rd

Computes the necessary sample size for the confidence interval on a population reliability coefficient (coefficient alpha or coefficient omega, depending on the assumed measurement model) to have expected width no larger than width, or (when assurance is supplied) to be no wider than width with the specified probability. This is the accuracy in parameter estimation (AIPE) counterpart to power based planning for reliability and is the companion of reliability. Without an assurance the sample size comes from a closed form for the expected width of the interval type names: the normal theory variance of coefficient alpha of van Zyl, Neudecker, and Nel (2000) for the parallel model and for the normal theory interval of the tau equivalent model (Terry & Kelley, 2012, Eq. 19), and the delta method variance of the model implied coefficient for the factor analytic interval of the tau equivalent model (equal loadings) and for the congeneric model (coefficient omega). When assurance is supplied, a Monte Carlo search starting from the closed form finds the smallest N delivering the requested assurance (Terry & Kelley, 2012).

Coefficient alpha (Guttman, 1945; subsequently popularized by Cronbach, 1951) is planned for under the parallel and tau equivalent (i.e., the so called True Score) measurement models; coefficient omega (McDonald, 1999) is planned for under the congeneric model. The coefficient is the one reliability_alpha and reliability_omega estimate from the raw item scores: the population, however it is given, is used as a covariance matrix, so items of unequal variance are planned for as they are, and a correlation matrix plans for standardized items.

When the coefficient will be estimated from incomplete data by full information maximum likelihood, the interval at a given N is wider than it would be with complete data. The fmi argument plans for that: it is the fraction of missing information anticipated for the coefficient, and the plan grows to carry the information that complete data would have carried (see the section on planning under missing data).

Usage

ss_aipe_reliability(
  model = NULL,
  type = NULL,
  width = NULL,
  true_cov_matrix = NULL,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  assurance = NULL,
  data = NULL,
  n_items = NULL,
  true_item_covariance = NULL,
  true_factor_loading = NULL,
  true_residual_var = NULL,
  G_initial = 500,
  G = 5000,
  start_N = NULL,
  verbose = FALSE,
  fmi = 0,
  seed = NULL
)

Arguments

model

The measurement model assumed for the population. Accepts (case-sensitive aliases shown in parentheses): "Parallel" ("parallel", "SB", "Spearman Brown", "Spearman-Brown", "sb") for the strictly parallel items model; "True Score" ("True Score Equivalent", "True-Score Equivalent", "Equivalent", "Tau Equivalent", "tau-equivalent", "Tau-Equivalent", "True-Score", "true-score", "true score", "Cronbach", "cronbach", "Chronbach", "alpha") for the tau equivalent model (in which case the function plans for coefficient alpha); or "Congeneric" ("congeneric", "omega", "Omega") for the congeneric model (in which case the function plans for coefficient omega).

type

The method used to construct the confidence interval on the reliability coefficient: either "Factor Analytic" (McDonald, 1999), available for all three measurement models, or "Normal Theory" (van Zyl, Neudecker, & Nel, 2000), available for the parallel and tau equivalent models only (with the congeneric model it is an error).

width

The desired full width of the two-sided confidence interval.

true_cov_matrix

A symmetric population covariance matrix among the items (a planning value, not a sample covariance matrix), used as it is to imply the population reliability and its sampling distribution; a matrix with a negative eigenvalue is refused. A correlation matrix is a covariance matrix of standardized items and plans for them.

conf_level

Confidence level (i.e., \(1 - \alpha\), where \(\alpha\) is the Type I error rate). Default 0.95.

assurance

Optional probability with which the realized interval is to be no wider than width (a sample that returns no interval counts as one that is wider). When NULL (the default), the planner targets the expected width; when supplied (e.g., 0.80, 0.85, 0.95), the function follows the closed form with a Monte Carlo search.

data

A data set from which the population covariance matrix should be inferred, from its complete cases; the number of items is the number of its columns.

n_items

Number of items (J in the formulas of the Details). Needed when the population is given by true_item_covariance or true_factor_loading with true_residual_var; with true_cov_matrix or data it is the number of columns and need not be given.

true_item_covariance

The presumed common covariance c of every pair of items, which with true_residual_var gives the population: the common loading is the square root of c, so two items covary c and an item's variance is c plus its true_residual_var. It is the inter-item correlation of Terry and Kelley (2012) when the items are standardized, that is, when true_residual_var is \(1 - c\); otherwise items j and k correlate \(c / \sqrt{(c + \psi^2_j)(c + \psi^2_k)}\), with \(\psi^2_j\) the residual variance of item j. With true_item_covariance = .3 and true_residual_var = .2, for example, the items correlate .6, not .3. One value.

true_factor_loading

Population factor loading or loadings: one number for the Parallel and True Score models, whose items share one loading, and a vector of n_items loadings for the Congeneric model. A vector for the Parallel or True Score model is an error that names the Congeneric model, since unequal loadings are what distinguish it.

true_residual_var

Population residual (unique, or error) variance or variances: one number for the Parallel model, whose items share one, and a vector of n_items variances for the True Score and Congeneric models, each greater than zero; with the normal theory interval of the True Score model, any values that leave the covariance matrix they imply a covariance matrix (see Details).

G_initial

Number of Monte Carlo replications in each pass of the initial assurance search (default 500): a single whole number of at least 1.

G

Number of Monte Carlo replications in each pass of the final assurance verification (default 5000), the count the reported assurance_attained rests on: a single whole number of at least 1. Anything else given for either count is refused with an error of class dmar_count_invalid. Neither is used without assurance.

start_N

Optional starting total sample size for the iterative assurance search.

verbose

If TRUE, prints the current sample size and empirical assurance at each step of the Monte Carlo search.

fmi

The fraction of missing information anticipated for the reliability coefficient when it is estimated by full information maximum likelihood from incomplete data: a single number in \([0, 1)\), with the default 0 for complete data, which returns exactly the complete data plan. It is not the proportion of missing values. Writing \(\gamma\) for fmi, the plan divides the complete data \(N - 1\) by \(1 - \gamma\); see the section on planning under missing data for the derivation and for where a planning value comes from.

seed

Optional seed for the Monte Carlo assurance search. The default NULL draws from the current state of the random number generator; a number makes the search reproducible, and the caller's generator state is restored when the function returns. The closed form (no assurance) draws nothing.

Value

A data.frame with columns term and value. Without assurance the data frame has a single row, "necessary_N", giving the necessary N. With assurance supplied, the data frame has five rows: "necessary_N" (necessary N), "width" (echo of the target width), "assurance" (echo of the requested probability), "assurance_attained" (the assurance achieved at the returned N in the Monte Carlo verification), and "G" (the number of Monte Carlo replications of the final pass). When fmi is above 0, necessary_N is the size under missing data, the rows are otherwise unchanged, and two attributes record the plan: fmi, the value planned for, and necessary_N_complete, the size complete data would need (for the closed form, its solution rounded up, while the plan maps the unrounded solution; for an assurance plan, the size at which the assurance was simulated, so assurance_attained refers to it). With fmi = 0 neither attribute is added. An assurance plan carries the number of samples of its final Monte Carlo pass that returned no interval as the no_interval attribute (zero when every sample returned one), printed under the table when above zero; they are counted as wide in assurance_attained. Both forms carry the class dmar_ss_aipe of the AIPE planners: generics::tidy() gives the planned N, beside the target width for an assurance plan (the closed form's table holds only necessary_N, so its width is NA), and generics::glance() adds the remaining rows as columns, and the fmi, necessary_N_complete, and no_interval attributes when the plan has them (see dmar_tidiers).

Details

The closed forms. Each closed form takes the sampling variance of the coefficient to be \(V / (N - 1)\) and solves \(2 z \sqrt{V / (N - 1)} = w\) for N, so that \(N = 4 z^2 V / w^2 + 1\), where w is width and z the standard normal quantile for conf_level. For the parallel model V is the compound symmetry form \(2 (1 - \alpha)^2 J / (J - 1)\) of van Zyl et al. (2000), with J items, which at a population of parallel items is also the variance of the factor analytic interval, so the parallel model has one closed form for both types. For the normal theory interval of the tau equivalent model V is the general variance of alpha of van Zyl et al. (Terry & Kelley, 2012, Eqs. 7, 8, and 19), evaluated on the population covariance matrix as the formula defines it. For the congeneric model V is the delta method variance of the model implied omega, \(\omega = (\sum \lambda_j)^2 / ((\sum \lambda_j)^2 + \sum \psi_j^2)\), with \(\lambda_j\) the loadings (true_factor_loading) and \(\psi_j^2\) the error variances (true_residual_var): the gradient of omega taken through the inverse of the expected information of the single-factor model at the population (Raykov, 2002; Terry & Kelley, 2012, Eqs. 13 to 16), the variance behind reliability_omega(denominator = "model_implied", ci_method = "ml"), whose squared standard error is \(V / N\); taking it as \(V / (N - 1)\), as for alpha, adds one case and keeps the planning under missing data below the same for every model. When the population is given by true_cov_matrix or data, the single-factor model is first fit to it by maximum likelihood. Terry and Kelley (2012, p. 390) had no closed form for omega: they used the alpha formula as if true score equivalence held only as a starting value, and found the size whose mean interval width met the target by an a priori Monte Carlo simulation. That starting value, taken as the plan for omega, is too large when the loadings differ among standardized items and can be far too small when the item variances differ. The delta method form gives the expected width to first order. The mean width of the factor analytic interval at the planned N meets the target where the samples at that N stay away from an improper solution and from empirical underidentification, and exceeds it where some do not, whose intervals are far wider, while the median width stays near the target (within 4 percent of it in the simulations below, above it in some). Which samples come near depends on the loadings, the number of items, and N together, so no bound on the loadings alone marks the populations the closed form serves. With three items the single-factor model is just identified, each squared loading is a ratio of the covariances (\(\lambda_1^2 = \sigma_{12} \sigma_{13} / \sigma_{23}\)), and a sample covariance near zero makes the solution run away: three loadings of .3 planned for a width of .20 take 687 cases, at which the median width is .202 and the mean .264, and 3 percent of samples give no interval (1,000 samples), while at a width of .10 (2743 cases) the mean is on target; loadings of .5, .4, and .3 at .20 (462 cases) average .242, with a median of .206, and three loadings of .4 (468 cases) .211, with a median of .199 (500 samples each). With four loadings of .3 the mean width was on target at .20 (527 cases) but averaged .323 at .30 (235 cases), where a tenth of the samples give no interval. Where the factor rests on weak loadings the same happens with more items: loadings of .7, .7, .1, and .1 (omega .46) planned for a width of .10 take 974 cases, at which the median width is .104 and the mean .181, and four loadings of .15 take 3437 cases, with a median of .098 and a mean of .148. In the other populations simulated for this planner, with four or more items whose loadings share a sign, the mean was within a few percent of the target (for loadings of opposite sign, see below). For a population like those above, plan with an assurance above .5, whose search counts the widths themselves.

For the factor analytic interval of the tau equivalent model V is the same delta method variance with the loadings held equal, the variance behind reliability_alpha(estimator = "model_implied", ci_method = "ml"): the single loading's information is the sum of the loading block of the information above, and its gradient the sum of the loadings' gradients. That coefficient is the maximum likelihood estimator under the model, so its variance is no larger than the normal theory variance of alpha, and it is smaller whenever the error variances differ: with loadings .7 and error variances .1, .2, 1, and 2, a width of .10 takes 242 cases with the factor analytic interval and 367 with the normal theory one. With equal error variances the two coincide.

Populations that are refused. The planning population has to be one the model describes. A population given as true_cov_matrix must be a covariance matrix (no negative eigenvalue), and when the single-factor model is fit to it, the fit must be proper. Where that model is fit, for the congeneric model and for the tau equivalent model with the factor analytic interval, every error variance in true_residual_var must be above zero, as the parallel model requires: a negative one is not a variance, and a zero one makes an item free of error, the boundary at which the single-factor solution is improper. The same population given as true_cov_matrix is refused through its fit. With the normal theory interval of the tau equivalent model nothing is fit: the loading and the error variances only build the covariance matrix the plan is made from, which must be a covariance matrix, as true_cov_matrix must, and the plan is the one the same matrix given as true_cov_matrix gives. The congeneric model needs at least three items with a nonzero loading, without which it is not identified at the population and omega has no sampling variance. With the factor analytic interval of the parallel and tau equivalent models, items to which the single-factor model with equal loadings gives a loading of zero share no common factor in that model, and the coefficient that interval estimates is zero, on the boundary of its range, where the closed form does not describe the interval. For a population given by its loading (true_item_covariance or true_factor_loading) that is a loading of zero, and for one given as true_cov_matrix or data the loading of the maximum likelihood fit. For items of equal variance it happens exactly when their covariances average zero or below (alpha of the population matrix at or below zero); with unequal variances the fit weighs each covariance by the inverse of its two items' variances, and the two can disagree either way (three items of variance 1 that correlate .3 and a fourth of variance 4 that correlates -.25 with them have alpha -0.276 and a fitted coefficient of .315, which the tau equivalent model plans for). The parallel model's closed form is a function of alpha of the population matrix, and it is refused when alpha is at or below zero; a population whose fitted coefficient is nonetheless positive is far from parallel, and the message names the tau equivalent model. A supplied population under model = "Parallel" must have equal diagonal entries and equal off-diagonal entries, each within \(\sqrt{\epsilon}\max |S|\), where \(\epsilon\) is machine precision. This check uses the original item units. A sample covariance will generally depart from an exact parallel population; specify the intended population with true_factor_loading and true_residual_var when parallelism is a planning assumption rather than a property of true_cov_matrix.

Where the congeneric closed form is refused. The delta method takes omega, a square of the sum of the loadings \(L\) over the variance of the composite, to be normal with its first-order variance, which needs \(L\) to be large relative to its standard error. When it is not, as when loadings of opposite sign nearly cancel in the unweighted sum, omega behaves near zero as the square of a normal variable, and its first-order variance understates the width of its interval; where the loadings cancel exactly, the gradient of omega vanishes and the closed form gives one case. The closed form is therefore checked at the N it gives, or at n_items + 1 cases when it gives fewer, the fewest at which the factor analytic interval can be computed (with fewer, the sample covariance matrix is singular). Write \(\sigma_L\) for the standard error of \(\hat L\) there, \(r = \sigma_L / |L|\), and \(P\) for the sum of the error variances. Near zero \(\hat\omega\) is about \(\hat L^2 / P\) and its delta method standard error about \(2 |\hat L| \sigma_L / P\), so with \(\hat L\) normal, the interval the estimation functions report, clamped at zero, averages $$\frac{E[\min(4 z |X|, X^2 + 2 z |X|)]}{4 z / r}, \qquad X \sim N(1 / r, 1),$$ times the width planned for. That ratio stays below one, the clamped interval making the plan conservative, until \(r\) is about 1.5 at 95 percent confidence (1.36 at 90 percent and 1.66 at 99), and it exceeds one beyond; the closed form is refused once it does. In simulations of the factor analytic interval at the planned N for loadings .7, -.7, .5, and a fourth loading of -.2, -.32, -.35, or -.37 (\(r\) of .41, 1.07, 1.52, and 2.00 there, the last two refused), the mean width was .082, .082, .089, and .121 for a target of .10. With a fourth loading of -.4 (omega .0038, \(r = 3.35\)) the closed form's 49 cases give a mean width of .22, where the interval needs about 95, and with -.5 the loadings cancel and the delta method gives one case. An assurance plan is not refused: its search counts the widths of the intervals themselves, starting at no fewer than n_items + 1 cases. A congeneric closed form below n_items + 1 is floored at that size before any missing-information inflation, with a warning. This is only a feasibility minimum. It does not establish that the expected width target is met at such a small sample size; an assurance plan is recommended.

Whenever the loadings of a congeneric population differ in sign, the planner warns. An item that loads opposite to the others lowers omega of the unweighted sum, as an item keyed in the opposite direction does when it is not reverse scored. The plan is for omega of the sum of the items as they are given; reverse score such items before planning, as before the coefficient is estimated.

The parallel and tau equivalent models need no such check. Their one loading enters the covariance matrix only through its square, the common covariance, of which their coefficient is a smooth function, so its variance does not vanish near zero, and there the clamped interval only makes the plan conservative: four parallel items that covary .03 (alpha .11) planned for a width of .30 take 362 cases, at which the factor analytic interval averages .236 wide.

The assurance search. The Monte Carlo search draws samples from the population covariance matrix and, at each candidate sample size, computes the realized confidence interval width with the same machinery the estimation side of the package uses. For type = "Factor Analytic" the single-factor model is fit by maximum likelihood (equal loadings for the parallel and tau equivalent models, free loadings for the congeneric model) and the interval is the delta method Wald interval on the model implied reliability, the interval of reliability_omega(denominator = "model_implied", ci_method = "ml") and of reliability_alpha(estimator = "model_implied", ci_method = "ml"). For type = "Normal Theory" the interval uses the van Zyl, Neudecker, and Nel (2000) closed form standard error for the tau equivalent model and its compound symmetry simplification for the parallel model, the same closed form behind reliability_alpha(ci_method = "ml"). The congeneric model has no normal theory form, so type = "Normal Theory" is an error there.

The search starts from the closed form size, and with the factor analytic interval at no fewer than n_items + 1 cases, the fewest whose sample covariance matrix the single-factor model can be fit to (a highly reliable population planned for a wide interval can have a closed form below that). When that size falls short of the assurance, the size is raised one case at a time until a pass of G_initial samples meets it, and a final pass of G samples confirms the size, again raising it if needed (Terry & Kelley, 2012). When the closed form size already meets the assurance, which happens when the assurance is near one half or below, or when the interval of type is narrower than the one the closed form describes (as the factor analytic interval of the parallel model can be when the population given as true_cov_matrix or data is not parallel), the search moves down: to the size at which the widths it has drawn would just meet the target (the width of a Wald interval shrinks as \(1 / \sqrt{N - 1}\)), and from there up one case at a time to the first size that meets it.

Each sample is treated as the estimation functions treat it, so the search counts the intervals a user would be given. A sample for which reliability_omega or the model implied reliability_alpha would return no interval (a single-factor fit that does not converge, three items with no single-factor solution, or a solution that has run away, whose error variances sum below zero so that the model implied coefficient is above one; McDonald, 2004) gave no interval, and so no narrow one: it is counted as wider than width. So is a sample whose likelihood has no maximum, whatever the sum, one error variance running off below zero while the likelihood is flat or still rising, which the estimation functions refuse with an error of class dmar_no_maximum (see reliability_omega). The assurance is the probability that the study yields an interval no wider than width (Terry & Kelley, 2012, p. 373), not that probability among the studies that yield an interval. When some samples of the final pass returned no interval, the result says how many (the no_interval attribute, printed under the table), since at the planned N that share of studies would end without a coefficient. Each confidence limit is clamped into [0, 1], as the estimation functions clamp it, so a negative alpha whose interval lies wholly below zero has the interval [0, 0]. A size at which no sample returns an interval stops the search with the first error.

The cost of the assurance search depends on the interval. The normal theory intervals are closed forms, so a search at the default G_initial = 500 and G = 5000 finishes in seconds. With the factor analytic interval a one factor model is fit at every Monte Carlo iteration and at every candidate sample size the search visits, so a congeneric plan with an assurance runs for tens of seconds even at G_initial = 50 and G = 200 and for many minutes at the defaults. The examples on this page therefore stop at the closed form for the congeneric plan; the assurance version is the same call with assurance supplied (for example, assurance = .80). A seed makes the search reproducible and leaves the caller's random number stream as it was; without one the search draws from, and advances, the current stream.

Note

Not all of the items can be entered into the function to represent the population values. For example, either data can be used, or true_cov_matrix, or n_items, true_item_covariance, and true_residual_var, or n_items, true_factor_loading, and true_residual_var. With a large number of replications (G) this function may take considerable time.

Planning Under Missing Data

The fraction of missing information (FMI) of a parameter is $$\gamma = 1 - \frac{SE_C^2}{SE_O^2},$$ where \(SE_O\) is the standard error of the estimate from the data as observed and \(SE_C\) the standard error the same sample would have given had it been complete (Savalei & Rhemtulla, 2012, Eq. 4). It is the proportion of the information about the parameter that the missing values take away, one minus the asymptotic efficiency of the incomplete data estimator relative to the complete data one. At a fixed N, missing values therefore multiply the sampling variance of the estimate by \(1 / (1 - \gamma)\) and the width of a Wald interval by \(1 / \sqrt{1 - \gamma}\), the width inflation factor of Savalei and Rhemtulla (2012); an FMI of .56 makes the interval 1.5 times as wide.

Every closed form on this page has a sampling variance of the form \(V / (N - 1)\), so its information about the coefficient is \((N - 1) / V\). With missing data that information becomes \((N - 1)(1 - \gamma) / V\), and the width target is met when \((N - 1)(1 - \gamma)\) equals \(N_c - 1\), where \(N_c\) is the complete data solution of the closed form before it is rounded up to a whole number: $$N = \frac{N_c - 1}{1 - \gamma} + 1.$$ The factor scales \(N - 1\) rather than N because \(N - 1\) is what the planner's information is proportional to; the target sample size of Savalei and Rhemtulla (2012), \(N / (1 - \gamma)\), is the same idea for an information proportional to N, and the two differ by \(\gamma / (1 - \gamma)\) cases (one case at an FMI of .5). An FMI of .5 doubles \(N - 1\), not N. The plan is the smallest whole N at or above that value. The complete data sample size, the whole number \(N_c\) rounds up to, travels with the result as the necessary_N_complete attribute and is printed under the table. Because the plan maps the unrounded \(N_c\), the formula applied to the printed whole number can give a larger N than the plan, by up to about \(1 / (1 - \gamma)\) cases (the population of the first example below needs 38 cases with complete data and 42 at an FMI of .1, while the formula applied to 38 gives 43).

With an assurance, the Monte Carlo search runs exactly as it does for complete data, starting from the complete data closed form, and the size \(N_e\) it finds is mapped back with the same formula. The search therefore takes the distribution of the interval width at N under missing data to be the complete data width distribution at the effective size \((N - 1)(1 - \gamma) + 1\), which keeps the larger relative variability of the widths of a smaller sample (scaling the complete data widths at N by the width inflation factor would not). This is a first-order approximation, and ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity checks it by simulating incomplete data and analyzing them by full information maximum likelihood (its fmi and missing_prop arguments). The assurance_attained row is the assurance found at \(N_e\), the necessary_N_complete attribute is \(N_e\) itself (a whole number, so the formula applied to it reproduces the plan), and a start_N is read as a size under missing data and converted to its effective size before the search.

Where the FMI comes from. The FMI belongs to the coefficient, not to the items, and it is not the proportion of missing values: it depends on the missing data mechanism, the model, and how strongly the items are related. Information lost on one item is partly recovered from the items correlated with it, so the FMI can be lower than the rate of missing data; under data missing completely at random it is bounded by the largest rates of univariate and pairwise missingness, and under data missing at random it can be well above the rate of missing data (Savalei & Rhemtulla, 2012). At the design stage it comes from a pilot study or a comparable data set analyzed the way the planned study will be: fit the single-factor model by full information maximum likelihood (for example fa_confirmatory(..., missing = "fiml", output = "fit"), with equal_loading = TRUE for the tau equivalent coefficient that the Parallel and True Score plans target) and take the FMI of its omega_ defined parameter from fraction_missing_information. That FMI refers to the cases the fit used: a case with no observed item carries no information, and the fit sets it aside (the N_excluded attribute counts such cases). When the planned N counts every case recruited, those who will answer no item included, fold them in as \(1 - (N_{used} / N)(1 - \gamma)\), with \(N_{used}\) the cases the fit used and N those recruited; ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity reports the FMI its simulated data realized in the same way. A sample FMI is imprecise. Chen and Savalei (2021) found it close to unbiased even at \(N = 50\) but variable from sample to sample: precise estimates took several hundred cases at overall missing rates of 10 to 20 percent and more than 1,000 at 30 percent. Planning with the upper limit of an interval for the pilot's FMI, rather than with its point estimate, is the conservative choice. Von Hippel (2020) recommends the same use of a pilot's upper limit when deciding how many imputations to run; carrying it over to sample size planning is our extension.

Two things fmi leaves alone. The data argument still estimates the planning covariance matrix from the complete cases of the pilot data (na.omit()); fmi is what carries the missing data of the planned study. And the planned interval is the same Wald interval with a normal critical value; the FMI changes how much information the sample carries, not the reference distribution.

Warning

In some conditions the factor analytic model fit by cfa_1 (via lavaan) may fail to converge, and you may see a non-convergence message from lavaan. The Monte Carlo assurance search counts a non-converged iteration as an interval wider than width and continues, and the number of such iterations in the final pass is printed under the result; a sample size at which no iteration converges stops the search with the first error. Frequent non-convergence usually means the model is poorly determined by the data, for example because of a small sample size or a poorly behaved covariance matrix, and it raises the planned N, since a study that yields no interval has not yielded a narrow one.

Terry, L. J., & Kelley, K. (2012). Sample size planning for composite reliability coefficients: Accuracy in parameter estimation via narrow confidence intervals. British Journal of Mathematical and Statistical Psychology, 65, 371–401. doi:10.1111/j.2044-8317.2011.02030.x

van Zyl, J. M., Neudecker, H., & Nel, D. G. (2000). On the distribution of the maximum likelihood estimator of Cronbach's alpha. Psychometrika, 65(3), 271–280. doi:10.1007/BF02296146

von Hippel, P. T. (2020). How many imputations do you need? A two-stage calculation using a quadratic rule. Sociological Methods & Research, 49(3), 699–718. doi:10.1177/0049124117747303

See also

reliability, cfa_1, ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity to check a plan, under complete or missing data, by simulation.

design_consequences for what a chosen design delivers: power, the Type S (sign) and Type M (exaggeration) errors of the significance filter, and the expected confidence interval width.

Author

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu

Examples

# Expected confidence interval width (closed form, no Monte Carlo search)
# for six parallel items that correlate .6: standardized items, so
# true_residual_var is 1 - true_item_covariance.
ss_aipe_reliability(model = "Parallel", type = "Normal Theory", width = .1,
  n_items = 6, true_item_covariance = .6, true_residual_var = .4,
  conf_level = .95, assurance = NULL)
#>  term        value
#>  necessary_N 38   
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# The same plan when the coefficient will be estimated by full information
# maximum likelihood and is expected to lose 30 percent of its information
# to missing values (an FMI of .30 from a pilot study). The complete data
# N minus 1 is divided by 1 minus .30, and the complete data answer prints
# under the table.
ss_aipe_reliability(model = "Parallel", type = "Normal Theory", width = .1,
  n_items = 6, true_item_covariance = .6, true_residual_var = .4,
  conf_level = .95, fmi = .30)
#>  term        value
#>  necessary_N 54   
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
#> 
#> Planned for a fraction of missing information of 0.3 for the coefficient; with complete data, N = 38.

# The assurance cases run a Monte Carlo search. G_initial = 20 and
# G = 100 keep the examples quick; a reported plan deserves the
# defaults of 500 and 5000. The seed makes each search reproducible and
# leaves the random number stream of the session where it was.

# Same population, now targeting an assurance.
ss_aipe_reliability(model = "Parallel", type = "Normal Theory", width = .1,
  n_items = 6, true_item_covariance = .6, true_residual_var = .4,
  conf_level = .95, assurance = .85, G_initial = 20, G = 100, seed = 113)
#>  term               value
#>  necessary_N        54   
#>  width              0.100
#>  assurance          0.850
#>  assurance_attained 0.860
#>  G                  100  
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# The assurance plan under the same FMI. The search runs at the complete
# data size, the necessary N of the call above (kept as the attribute
# necessary_N_complete), and maps it back.
ss_aipe_reliability(model = "Parallel", type = "Normal Theory", width = .1,
  n_items = 6, true_item_covariance = .6, true_residual_var = .4,
  conf_level = .95, assurance = .85, G_initial = 20, G = 100, seed = 113,
  fmi = .30)
#>  term               value
#>  necessary_N        77   
#>  width              0.100
#>  assurance          0.850
#>  assurance_attained 0.860
#>  G                  100  
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
#> 
#> Planned for a fraction of missing information of 0.3 for the coefficient; with complete data, N = 54, the size at which the assurance was simulated.

# The true score (tau equivalent) model takes true_residual_var as a
# vector of length n_items (number of items) while true_item_covariance
# stays a single value. Error
# variances around 1 - .5 give item variances from .9 to 1.1 and
# correlations near .5, and the plan is for alpha of these items as they
# are, unequal variances and all.
ss_aipe_reliability(model = "True Score", type = "Normal Theory",
  width = .1, n_items = 5, true_item_covariance = .5,
  true_residual_var = c(.4, .5, .6, .4, .6),
  conf_level = .95, assurance = .85, G_initial = 20, G = 100,
  seed = 113)
#>  term               value
#>  necessary_N        137  
#>  width              0.100
#>  assurance          0.850
#>  assurance_attained 0.860
#>  G                  100  
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# Congeneric model, planned from the item loadings and error variances rather
# than from a single covariance. With assurance = NULL the necessary N comes
# from the delta method variance of the model implied omega at the
# population, the variance behind reliability_omega(denominator =
# "model_implied", ci_method = "ml"). Adding an assurance to this plan fits
# a one factor model at every Monte Carlo iteration and is the slow case,
# so the page stops at the closed form (see Details).
ss_aipe_reliability(model = "Congeneric", type = "Factor Analytic", width = .15,
  n_items = 4, true_factor_loading = c(.8, .7, .7, .8),
  true_residual_var = c(.4, .5, .5, .4),
  conf_level = .95, assurance = NULL)
#>  term        value
#>  necessary_N 52   
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# Planning from a presumed population correlation matrix among the items,
# which plans for standardized items.
pop_mat <- rbind(
  c(1.0000000, 0.3813850, 0.4216370, 0.3651484, 0.4472136),
  c(0.3813850, 1.0000000, 0.4020151, 0.3481553, 0.4264014),
  c(0.4216370, 0.4020151, 1.0000000, 0.3849002, 0.4714045),
  c(0.3651484, 0.3481553, 0.3849002, 1.0000000, 0.4082483),
  c(0.4472136, 0.4264014, 0.4714045, 0.4082483, 1.0000000))
ss_aipe_reliability(model = "True Score", type = "Normal Theory", width = .15,
  true_cov_matrix = pop_mat, conf_level = .95, assurance = .85,
  G_initial = 20, G = 100, seed = 113)
#>  term               value
#>  necessary_N        113  
#>  width              0.150
#>  assurance          0.850
#>  assurance_attained 0.890
#>  G                  100  
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
